subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Representativeness Heuristic
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Representativeness Heuristic.

hook.text: She's quiet and wears glasses. People guess librarian over salesperson despite 75x more salespeople.

buildup.text: We judge likelihood by how well someone fits a stereotype, not by actual statistical frequency.

discovery.text: Representativeness heuristic: if it looks like a duck, we call it a duck, ignoring the base rates.

twist.text: Coin flip HHHTTT feels 'less random' than HTTHHT, but both are equally probable sequences.

climax.text: Stereotypes feel accurate because they match patterns. But matching a pattern doesn't make it likely.

punchline.text: Looking the part doesn't mean playing it.

quiz.question: What does the representativeness heuristic cause us to do?
options: Judge by how well something fits a stereotype

details.summary: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity: how much something resembles a typical example of a category. This leads to base rate neglect, conjunction fallacies, and stereotyping because resemblance is confused with likelihood.
details.whyItMatters: Representativeness drives many systematic errors in judgment by replacing probability with similarity. People stereotype, see patterns in randomness, and make probability errors because they ask 'how similar' instead of 'how likely.'
takeaways: People judge probability by how much something resembles a stereotype
Similarity-based judgment leads to systematic probability errors
Base rates and sample sizes are ignored when representativeness dominates

faq.question: How does the representativeness heuristic cause errors?
faq.answer: It makes people judge a quiet, bookish person as more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians. The person fits the librarian stereotype, so representativeness overrides the base rate.

faq.question: Can the representativeness heuristic ever be useful?
faq.answer: Yes. When base rates are roughly equal and stereotypes are statistically accurate, representativeness provides a fast and reasonable heuristic. The problems arise when it is used in situations where base rates are very unequal or stereotypes are inaccurate.
